item.title: Investigators Search for Answers After 5 Were Killed in Runway Crash
item.description:
Investigators in Miami searched for clues on Monday one day after five people were killed and five were injured when a cargo plane overran a runway upon landing and struck multiple vehicles.

The plane appeared to have overshot the end of the runway at Miami International Airport. It remained unclear Monday morning if the dead and injured had been on the plane or on the ground. The Miami-Dade County Fire Rescue chief, Raied Jadallah, said on Sunday that three of those injured were in critical condition and had been taken to a trauma center.

“What we found was a very complex situation here,” he said. Photos and videos taken on Sunday showed blackish smoke billowing from the partly damaged plane.

The National Transportation Safety Board was expected to provide a briefing on Monday. The authorities had not released the identities of the people who were killed as of Monday morning.

Miami-Dade Fire Rescue said more than 60 units had responded to the incident.

“Units arrived to find an airplane that had caught on fire as a result of this crash, with heavy flames and smoke showing,” the department said in a statement.

The Boeing 767-300 cargo aircraft departed from Luis Muñoz Marín International Airport in San Juan, Puerto Rico, and landed at the Miami airport around 2 p.m., the Federal Aviation Administration said in a statement.

Kelly Nantel, a spokeswoman for Amazon, said in a statement that an “Amazon Air plane operated by 21 Air experienced an incident while attempting to land” at the airport.

The crash happened during a busy Labor Day holiday weekend. The airport had more than 300 flights, outbound and inbound, that were delayed or canceled as of Sunday afternoon, according to FlightAware.com, which tracks flights. Disruptions continued into Monday morning, with at least 160 flights delayed and 65 canceled by around 11 a.m.

David Ovalle and Richard Fausset contributed reporting.

item.title: For Trump’s Former Fixer, a Tortured Path From ‘Rat’ to Reconciliation
item.description:
On a radio show last month, President Trump welcomed Michael D. Cohen, the former fixer he once denounced as a “rat” for testifying against him, back into the fold. “I respect the fact that you recanted everything you said,” Mr. Trump said. He went on to use the word “recant” three more times.

In case anyone missed it, the president posted a message on social media on Friday claiming that Mr. Cohen, a key witness against Mr. Trump in criminal and civil trials, “has just fully RECANTED his testimony.” Mr. Trump demanded “that any remnant of those Politically Weaponized Cases against me be immediately terminated and dismissed.”

Except Mr. Cohen has not, in fact, recanted his testimony. He has not taken any of it back.

In his eagerness to return to the president’s good graces, Mr. Cohen now says he “felt pressured and coerced” by prosecutors to testify. But he has not actually disavowed anything that he swore to under oath about Mr. Trump’s hush money scheme to cover up an affair with an adult film actress or about his former boss’s efforts to defraud his lenders.

And so this unlikeliest of rapprochements between two men who helped get each other convicted of crimes is built not on an emotional outpouring of forgiveness but on what looks like a pretty straightforward bargain, spoken or unspoken, according to people close to both. Mr. Trump is trying to use his former lawyer’s desire for absolution to rewrite history as he presses his effort to overturn his conviction. Mr. Cohen gets to position himself as an insider once again and possibly obtain a presidential pardon to wipe out his own felony record.

“Everything is transactional,” said Brian Karem, a journalist who helped Mr. Cohen write the second of his books assailing Mr. Trump. “It’s the weirdest example yet of the transactional nature of the president of the United States and those around him. Who knows him better than Michael? I’m just surprised that it took him this long. The first thing I said was, ‘Wow, it took you long enough.’”

Even in the long history of strange-bedfellow political alliances, this may be one of the strangest. To call the reconciliation between Mr. Trump and Mr. Cohen Shakespearean would not fully capture just how mind-boggling it really is. The Bard would have been hard pressed to come up with a scenario quite so far-fetched.

Mr. Trump, to be sure, has a well-known history of falling back in with people he has fallen out with (think Elon Musk, Stephen K. Bannon, Michael T. Flynn or, for that matter, his current vice president who once compared him to Hitler or his secretary of state who once questioned the size of his private parts).

But as one baffled Trump ally put it, Mr. Cohen is not someone who just trash-talked the president; he actually testified in court against him. Mr. Cohen went to prison because, he said, he committed crimes at the instructions of the man he now again calls “Boss.” And in a trial in which his onetime fixer provided evidence for the prosecution, Mr. Trump was convicted of 34 felonies that, had it not been for the intervening 2024 election, might have put him behind bars as well.

“You can’t write it,” said Donny Deutsch, a longtime New York advertising executive and television commentator who has been close with Mr. Cohen for years, reflecting the astonishment in both New York and Washington. “These two guys who were archenemies found mutual shared interest to get back in bed together.”

Mr. Deutsch said he did not blame Mr. Cohen, who in his view was collateral damage for Mr. Trump. “Michael was left by the side of the road as roadkill,” he said. “Beyond going to prison, he couldn’t practice law, he couldn’t get a job, he couldn’t get insurance. He’s doing what he needs to do to survive.”

As for Mr. Trump, accepting Mr. Cohen back into his orbit, even an outer orbit somewhere past Pluto, allows him to claim vindication. “If you go grovel to him and suck up to him, he loves that because it’s validation of his power,” said George T. Conway III, the former conservative lawyer who became one of Mr. Trump’s most vocal foes. “He has brought someone to heel. And part of what he does is try to intimidate people into doing that. He has a reptilian ability to sense who he can intimidate.”

Mr. Cohen did not respond to emails seeking comment. Mr. Trump posted his social media message on Friday about Mr. Cohen’s supposedly recanting about three hours after a request for comment was sent to the White House, which then passed along the link but otherwise did not respond to questions.

The relationship between these two men has arguably been one of the most consequential in modern presidential history. Mr. Cohen worked for Mr. Trump for years as his lawyer and fixer, a self-described “pit bull” who handled both business and personal problems and sought to intimidate people who got in the way. He styled himself as a consigliere so loyal that he famously said he would “do anything to protect Mr. Trump” including “take a bullet.”

Mr. Cohen secretly sought on Mr. Trump’s behalf to seal a deal with the Russians to build a Trump tower in Moscow even while his boss was running for president in 2016. He was the middle man who paid $130,000 to Stormy Daniels, the porn star, to buy her silence about her alleged tryst with Mr. Trump before the election. (Mr. Trump denies the affair.)

That eventually led to criminal charges, a guilty plea and prison. When Mr. Cohen was released, the Trump administration revoked his home confinement and locked him up again because he planned to publish a book, a move that a judge overruled because it was “retaliatory.”

Mr. Cohen later turned witness for Alvin L. Bragg, the Manhattan district attorney, in the case that convicted Mr. Trump for falsifying business records to cover up the payments to Ms. Daniels, as well as for Letitia James, the New York attorney general, in her civil case that found Mr. Trump liable for business fraud. His was not the only evidence against the president, and some lawyers argue that there was enough to convict Mr. Trump even without Mr. Cohen’s testimony.

But when Mr. Cohen broke from Mr. Trump, he broke big time. Not only did he testify in court, but he also went after the president publicly with both barrels, writing books titled “Disloyal” and “Revenge” and characterizing his former employer as “a racist,” “con man” and “cheat” during a congressional committee hearing.

Outside the halls of Congress, Mr. Cohen went even further, calling Mr. Trump “a mob boss,” “the slime of humanity,” a “scumbag,” a “petty tyrant,” a “deranged president,” a “narcissistic sociopath,” a “Cheeto-dusted cartoon villain,” “Dictator D-Bag,” “this Frankenstein’s monster” and “the poster boy for fascism” who was trying “to screw over the country.” And those were the lines printable in a family newspaper.

But by the time Mr. Trump won a second term, Mr. Cohen’s tone began to change. He had not gotten the pardon he had requested from President Joseph R. Biden Jr., nor had he been welcomed with open arms by the anti-Trump resistance. With Mr. Trump returning to office, any hope for acceptance, much less clemency, now lay with his former boss, and he has resubmitted his pardon application replacing the word “Biden” with “Trump.”

“I think he really wants a pardon,” said Stephanie Grisham, a former White House press secretary for Mr. Trump who broke with the president. “I also think he has realized just how hard it is to be on the wrong side of the administration. It’s damn scary out here on the anti-Trump island. And I never got the vibe from him that he wants to work hard at anything, and doing the right thing is never easy.”

In January 2025, just as Mr. Trump was assuming power again, Mr. Karem interviewed Mr. Cohen for a documentary that will be shown next month at the Chelsea Film Festival and asked if he would go back to Mr. Trump if invited.

“You know what, it’s such a difficult question to answer simply because, one, I know it’s never going to happen,” Mr. Cohen said in the film. “Donald refuses to accept any type of responsibility for anything. We’ve all seen that. Do I think I’m owed an explanation? Absolutely.”

Mr. Karem saw that as an implicit yes. “Anybody who spent any time talking with him back then, it was obvious that was open to him,” Mr. Karem said. “It was an avenue he was willing to explore because he felt wronged by the justice system. He wasn’t considered the hero he thought he would be. He told me he wanted a pardon.”

In the summer of 2025, Mr. Cohen had a brief conversation with Mr. Trump at his golf club in Bedminster, N.J., joined by the president’s top personal legal adviser, Boris Epshteyn, as The New York Times previously reported. By January 2026, Mr. Cohen was writing on Substack that “I felt pressured and coerced to only provide information and testimony that would satisfy the government’s desire” to convict Mr. Trump.

Two months later he reached out to Lara Trump, the president's daughter-in-law, who then invited him onto her podcast, where he defended Mr. Trump against those questioning his relationship with the disgraced financier and sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Soon, Mr. Cohen was given a radio slot on WABC by John Catsimatidis, the station’s owner and a longtime Trump supporter.

Even so, though, Mr. Cohen for a while kept a foot in both camps. Mr. Conway, who ran unsuccessfully for the Democratic nomination for a House seat in New York earlier this year, said Mr. Cohen volunteered to help his campaign.

“At the same time I’m reading these clips about him trying to get back in, he was calling me up saying, ‘I want to help you with your campaign. I want to help you with your campaign. Let’s go be seen together on the Upper East Side. People love me. It’ll help your campaign,’” Mr. Conway recalled. “I’m like, what? He’s trying to suck up to Trump and literally my entire campaign was about sending this guy to jail.”

His turnaround shocked people he had gotten to know on the left. Joanne Carducci, a liberal podcaster who had become friends with Mr. Cohen, said she was so upset that she cried, feeling that she had been fooled. “I trusted him, and I believed him when he said, ‘I’m done with that guy. I’ll never recover from what he did to me. I went to prison because of him,’” she recalled. “What is the pathology there that he could be so convincing?”

After Mr. Cohen’s Substack essay, Ms. Carducci texted to ask why he was now publicly helping Mr. Trump undermine the cases against him. “I have attacked him and the administration 998 out of 1000 times,” Mr. Cohen replied in a text that she shared with The Times. “James and Bragg, and the entire system is broken and abusive. That’s the point I was making. I’m not going to be a puppet as I lived the abuse.”

By all accounts, including his own, Mr. Cohen was crushed and embittered by the events of the past several years. His life, as he put it on his radio show, was “shredded to pieces,” and he lost his sense of purpose.

“I know what it feels like to take hit after soul-crushing hit, to be bloodied and knocked to the dirt while a crowd of millions cheers for your destruction and then, then, to have to pick up the shattered pieces of your life, alone in the dark while the circus packs up and moves on to its next victim,” he said on his show. “I know the sheer suffocating terror of being turned into a public target sitting in silence while your family weeps, wondering if you’re ever going to survive the night.”

And yet after all that, Mr. Cohen turned back to Mr. Trump. “People have their sect, their team,” said Greg Ehrlich, a onetime friend who recalls first introducing Mr. Cohen to Mr. Trump. “It’s your identity. His identity was Trump. Then he got lucky and had a second life, which was against Trump.” But now, Mr. Ehrlich said, “he needs his identity, and his identity was Donald Trump.”

Indeed, when they finally had their bury-the-hatchet talk on the radio last month, Mr. Cohen sounded needy, anxious to reminisce about the old times with the Boss, but the Boss wasn’t having any of it. Distant and hardly warm, Mr. Trump focused on promoting the fiction that Mr. Cohen had recanted his testimony, making clear that their reconciliation was dependent entirely on that. “You took it back,” Mr. Trump said falsely. “I wouldn’t even be talking to you right now if you didn’t, to be honest.”

Mr. Cohen did not correct Mr. Trump during the show. But in other appearances, he has stood by his accounts. Asked by Dan Abrams on SiriusXM radio if his criticism of prosecutors meant that his past testimony was not truthful, Mr. Cohen said: “No, to the exact contrary. As I stated, I felt pressured and coerced. That’s my personal feeling, which I am certainly entitled to have. In no way, shape or form should it connote that the information that I provided was anything but truthful and accurate.”

Stating otherwise, of course, could expose Mr. Cohen to criminal perjury charges, and it did not go unnoticed that he emphasized that he “felt” pressured, as opposed to saying that he actually was. When Jake Tapper said on CNN that Mr. Cohen had claimed that he was “pressured and coerced” into testifying against Trump, Mr. Cohen offered a word-parsing correction.

“The comment that I had written was in regard to Alvin Bragg and Tish James is that I felt pressured and coerced,” Mr. Cohen said. “And I think the distinction is extremely important.”

But that is a distinction without a difference for Mr. Trump. In the reality that the president is now selling, Mr. Cohen’s pivot is proof that Mr. Trump was innocent after all. Even if that is not what Mr. Cohen is actually saying.

item.title: Here’s What to Know About Amazon Air
item.description:
The airplane that overshot a runway in Miami on Sunday, killing five people and injuring five more, was a Boeing 767 operated for Amazon by 21 Air, a cargo airline.

Here’s what to know about those companies and the plane.

Amazon Air, the company’s cargo airline, is a key part of its worldwide shipping operation. Started in 2015, the airline leases planes to transport packages between dozens of airports in Asia, Europe, North America, the Middle East and Africa.

Amazon describes the airline as a “customer-obsessed” operation that runs more than 250 flights a day and can help shippers quickly move goods around the world. Amazon relies on the airline for its own shipping and sells excess capacity to other commercial customers.

Amazon Air contracts out its cargo flying, with about 105 planes actively operated for the company, according to Cirium, an aviation data company. 21 Air, which operated the plane that crashed Sunday, runs eight planes for Amazon. Air Transport International operates about 40 of those planes, and Sun Country Airlines, a budget carrier that also flies passengers, operates 22.

Amazon Air had one prior fatal crash. In February 2019, an Atlas Air cargo plane flying from Miami to Houston crashed into Texas’s Trinity Bay marshland, killing all three people on board. A federal investigation attributed that crash to pilot error.

21 Air is an all-cargo airline that was founded in North Carolina in 2014, according to its website. In addition to Amazon Air, 21 Air also flies for DHL Aviation, according to Cirium.

The airline flies mostly out of Miami and Cincinnati and describes its Boeing 767-300 aircraft, the plane type involved in the crash, as being able to carry 55 tons while delivering “excellent fuel efficiency.”

The plane that crashed was built in 1994, according to Cirium records.

Because commercial aircraft are inspected often and subject to frequent maintenance, it is not uncommon for planes to be used for decades, particularly by cargo airlines. The first 767 entered service in 1982, for United Airlines. There are nearly 900 still in active use today, mostly to carry cargo. About 200 are used mainly to carry passengers and a smaller number are used for military purposes.

While commercial plane crashes are rare, so-called runway excursions, in which an aircraft overshoots or otherwise leaves the bounds of a runway, are the most common form of accident reported each year, according to the International Air Transport Association, a global aviation trade association.

The causes of such incidents vary widely and can include wet or icy weather, unstable landings, runway contamination, pilot error, brake failures or other mechanical problems. It was not clear what caused Sunday’s accident.

item.title: What to Know About the Cargo Plane That Overran a Runway, Killing 5 in Miami
item.description:
A cargo plane overran a runway at Miami International Airport on Sunday afternoon, killing at least five people, injuring at least five others and snarling air travel for thousands of passengers during a busy holiday weekend.

The plane, operated for Amazon, had departed from Luis Muñoz Marín International Airport in San Juan, Puerto Rico, and touched down in Miami just before 2 p.m., according to the Federal Aviation Administration.

The incident cast a pall over Miami and its airport, an important gateway connecting South Florida to the rest of the world. The airport, about 10 miles from downtown Miami, is the nation’s busiest for international freight, according to its website, and generates $212 billion annually in business revenue.

Here’s what to know about the crash.

The plane overran a runway and then crashed into multiple vehicles, officials said. It was not clear Sunday afternoon whether those killed had been aboard the plane or were on the ground.

Raied Jadallah, chief of Miami-Dade Fire-Rescue, said several people were trapped inside their vehicles. A person who arrived afterward described some of the cars at the scene as “mangled.” Three injured people were in critical condition and were taken to a trauma center, Mr. Jadallah said.

Runway excursions — in which an aircraft overruns or otherwise leaves a runway during takeoff or landing — are the most common type of aviation accident reported annually, according to the International Air Transport Association, a global aviation trade group. They can happen for many reasons, including unstable approaches, runway conditions and crosswinds.

The cause of Sunday’s crash was not immediately apparent.

The cargo plane left a runway at Miami International Airport, about 10 miles from downtown Miami.

The airport is surrounded by warehouses, office parks and residential neighborhoods.

Another cargo plane crash killed five people at the same Miami airport in August 1997. A Fine Air DC-8 pitched sharply upward after takeoff, stalled and crashed into an open field. It burst into flames, skidded across a six-lane highway and into parking lot. The National Transportation Safety Board found that the plane’s cargo had been improperly loaded.

The plane was a Boeing 767-300 cargo aircraft built in 1994, according to Cirium records. It was operated for Amazon.

Amazon Air runs more than 250 flights a day, helping shippers quickly move packages around the world. The air cargo network is a key part of the company’s shipping operations.

Amazon Air contracts out its cargo flights. The plane that crashed on Sunday was operated by 21 Air, which operates eight planes for the company. 21 Air says the aircraft model involved in the crash can carry 55 tons and offers “excellent fuel efficiency.”

Thousands of passengers traveling during the Labor Day weekend had their flights delayed or canceled.

Officials stopped all arrivals and departures at Miami International shortly before 2 p.m. Two of the airport’s four runways reopened about three hours later. According to FlightAware, a flight-tracking website, at least 187 flights had been canceled and 266 had been delayed on Sunday.

Many travelers scrambled to book new tickets. Some headed to the airport in Fort Lauderdale, about an hour away.

Authorities had not released identities of those killed as of Sunday evening.

Johnny Diaz, Richard Fausset, Niraj Chokshi, Stacy Cowley, David Ovalle, Reshma Kirpalani, Bernard Mokam and McKinnon de Kuyper contributed reporting.

item.title: With a Gerrymander Vanquished, Wisconsin Democrats Aim for Control
item.description:
Sixteen years ago, Republicans in Wisconsin rode a national wave of discontent to wrest control of the legislature in Madison. Then they approved maps that locked in their power, even after Democrats took back nearly every statewide office.

This November, Democrats have a chance to do what seemed implausible a few short years ago: take control of the State Assembly and Senate while holding onto the governor’s mansion.

“I sincerely think this is the most important election that Wisconsin has ever seen,” said Dianne Hesselbein, the Democratic minority leader in the State Senate.

That is a well-worn, election-year trope but one the Democrats in Wisconsin may well believe. With a trifecta, Democrats would pivot away from a rightward shift defined by tax cuts, neutered labor unions and voter restrictions. It would also empower them to redraw a congressional map for 2028 to counter Republican gerrymandering threats throughout the South.

The reversal of fortune comes courtesy of a 2023 ruling by Wisconsin’s newly liberal State Supreme Court, which concluded that the Republicans’ legislative maps were unconstitutional and forced their replacement. In 2018, for instance, Democratic Assembly candidates won 53 percent of the vote across the state, but claimed only 36 of 99 seats.

Those maps made Wisconsin a case study in undemocratic gerrymandering. But after Republicans begrudgingly accepted maps proposed by Gov. Tony Evers, a Democrat, resurgent Democrats parlayed intense field organizing into big gains in 2024 — leaving them two seats shy of a State Senate majority, and five in the House.

Now, after the democratic socialist candidate Francesca Hong was defeated last month in the Democratic primary for governor, Democrats believe they can finish the job.

Robin Vos, the Republican speaker of the State Assembly whose power was once immense and who now plans to retire at year’s end, said 2026 always loomed as a challenging midterm election. President Trump is “a drag,” Mr. Vos said, adding that “some of the ways that he operates, not the policies per se, turn people off.”

Democrats hope to undo much of Mr. Vos’s legislative work.

“We’re just going to be passing bills that the residents want us to pass,” Ms. Hesselbein promised, citing affordability, health care and education.

Then, alluding to the divisive push in 2011 by the Republican former governor, Scott Walker, to strip public union bargaining rights, Ms. Hesselbein added: “We’re not going to be doing anything that’s going to bring 100,000 people protesting at the Capitol.”

If Democrats repeal that anti-collective bargaining act, hike school funding and create new entitlements, Mr. Vos warned, Wisconsin may go back to the discontent of 2009 and 2010 and multibillion-dollar deficits.

“I don’t think you can raise taxes enough to fund that,” he said.

Madison will look different next year regardless. For the first time ever, Wisconsin’s executive and legislative brass — Governor Evers, Mr. Vos, and Devin LeMahieu, the Senate majority leader — are retiring simultaneously.

In the governor’s primary in August, Mr. Evers helped David Crowley, the Milwaukee County executive, topple Ms. Hong, a state representative from Madison. Mr. Crowley now leads U.S. Representative Tom Tiffany, a staunch conservative, in the race to succeed Mr. Evers, according to a recent Marquette Law School poll.

Democrats are favored in generic polling for the legislature, where Republicans have a 54-to-45 advantage in the Assembly, and 18-to-15 in the Senate, according to the Marquette poll. But Republicans have a 2-to-1 financial advantage with $43 million raised, campaign finance reports show.

Three of the most competitive Assembly races are nestled within the Third Congressional District in western Wisconsin.

In the congressional race, Rebecca Cooke, a Democrat and a waitress with farm-country bona fides, is challenging U.S. Representative Derrick Van Orden, a fiery Trump loyalist, in a race that could prove pivotal to control of the U.S. House.

In La Crosse, Wis., Republicans are on offense, determined to unseat State Representative Steve Doyle, a 68-year-old lawyer who raises alpacas. Two years ago, he was Wisconsin’s only Democratic legislator to win a district carried by Mr. Trump.

Mr. Doyle was braced for attack ads tying him to Ms. Hong — “that would have been the thing I heard about the whole campaign,” he said. Instead, Mr. Doyle has hewed to a familiar routine, handing out pocket-size sports schedules — Packers, Badgers, NASCAR and hunting — touting a bipartisan record on taxes, health care and veterans issues, and talking up his website, MrBipartisan.com.

“Just an honest guy that is for normal people,” Linda Shiftar, a retired pharmacy technician, said of Mr. Doyle after he knocked on her door in Holmen, Wis.

Mr. Doyle’s opponent, Keith Purnell, a 63-year-old Army veteran, declined to be interviewed. But Mr. Vos, the longest-serving speaker in state history, said Republicans had recruited pragmatic center-right candidates.

“There’s nobody in Wisconsin that I think is yearning for a hard turn left or right,” he said.

Perhaps the most high-profile State Senate matchup is in the sprawling 17th District in the southwestern Driftless region, stretching from the Mississippi River bluffs to undulating cornfields just outside Madison. The current occupant, Howard Marklein, is co-chair of the powerful Joint Finance Committee.

His Democratic opponent, State Representative Jenna Jacobson, is a former financial analyst who criticizes Mr. Marklein and Republican leaders for failing to renew funding for outdoor recreation and land conservation projects.

Canvassing in Oregon, Wis., her hometown, Ms. Jacobson, 44, listened to constituents worried about the cost of living, “stopping Trump” and data centers.

Ms. Jacobson sought to regulate data centers’ water use and shield ratepayers, but the bill died. If Democrats win, she told Sue Capelle, a retired educator, “we can actually do some things that we just haven’t had leadership do recently.”

“Wouldn’t that be great?” Ms. Capelle sighed.

Mr. Marklein, 71, is campaigning frantically, too, after cruising to victory by as much as 20 points under the old maps. In Wiota and Monroe, Wis., he distributed a flier that repeated the word “rural” eight times.

Steve and Ron Buholzer, whose family has owned the Klondike Cheese Factory for generations, credited Mr. Marklein for easing regulations and improving rural roads for their trucks.

“Howard’s been a huge advocate,” Steve Buholzer said.

Mr. Marklein, a former accountant who grew up on a dairy farm in Spring Green — home to Frank Lloyd Wright’s Wisconsin refuge Taliesin — doesn’t always get his way. His proposal this year to spend the state’s surplus was torpedoed by Senate Democrats and conservative Republicans over structural deficit concerns. His proposal had been backed by Governor Evers, Ms. Jacobson and Mr. Doyle, all Democrats.

“You tell me I’m not bipartisan,” he said.

The surplus is now at $3 billion, and Mr. Marklein said he worried about Democratic control.

“I think it’s frightening,” he said after cooking steaks at an annual event supporting beef producers. “The fear that several people have is that we’ll become Minnesota.”

To Wisconsin Republicans, Democratic Minnesota is nothing to emulate, and not just because of the Vikings.

item.title: Bears in Los Angeles Are Getting Their Close-Ups, Ready or Not
item.description:
On hot days, they have their pick of swimming pools. They pluck avocados from backyard trees with impunity. When they amble down shaded streets, they are treated like celebrities: given a wide berth and photographed surreptitiously — except when they attract news helicopters.

They are California’s black bears, and there are, experts estimate, roughly 60,000 of them. Of the world’s eight bear species, including polar bears and giant pandas, the American black bear population is the only one that’s growing. In fact, there are more American black bears — omnivorous as raccoons and skittish around people — than bears of all other species combined.

In other words, the region’s bear population is thriving. It’s humans who have been left wrestling with how to adapt.

In recent years, black bears have expanded their range from remote mountains into suburbs that have increasingly blurred the line between city and wilderness.

Last year, officials with the state’s Department of Fish and Wildlife recorded 2,735 calls and reports about black bears. That’s up from 425 a decade prior, though they warned that the tally was skewed by changing tracking systems and staffing.

“Living alongside wildlife is a way of life in our foothill communities, but we’re seeing bears come into residential neighborhoods more frequently,” said Kathryn Barger, a Los Angeles County supervisor who represents the area. “Coming face to face with a 300-pound bear can be frightening, but in most cases these animals are simply looking to eat, cool off and move on.”

Researchers have found that a warming climate and wildfires may drive bears farther into human habitats. Across the country, similar shifts have prompted a cavalcade of wildlife tangles, like the peacocks that invaded a ritzy village in Florida, and the thousands of deer that overran an island off the coast of California.

But bears, with their fairy-tale associations and sheer size, stir unique fervor. And Californians, whose state flag immortalizes the image of a grizzly, which no longer roams in California, have the biggest bear population in the contiguous United States in their collective backyard.

“You’re going through that, like, roller coaster of fear and putting around cameras, and trying to haze them, and building fences and everything to protect ourselves,” said Brian Gordon, who lives in Monrovia, Calif., a leafy suburb tucked below the San Gabriel Mountains. “And after a couple months, realizing that it’s chill.”

Mr. Gordon and his partner started an Instagram account about what he describes as human and bear “co-thriving.” Their backyard pool has become a shrine to the “Pool Bear Life,” with a painting of a bear they call Maddie lounging in a hat and shades, a pink cocktail in her paw.

Others have a less whimsical take.

“I grew up seeing skunks, raccoons, possums,” said Ken Johnson, who has lived in Altadena, another Los Angeles County foothill community, for most of his life. In 2017, he saw a bear at his childhood home for the first time. It was sniffing around a bird feeder.

Then, in 2025, months after the deadly Eaton fire devastated Altadena, a mesh cover over Mr. Johnson’s crawl space was repeatedly chewed up. The day before Thanksgiving, a 500-pound black bear emerged.

“I was completely freaked out,” he said.

Mr. Johnson tried everything to evict the unwanted guest, who damaged ducts, causing a gas leak. He tried another crawl-space cover. He rigged cameras and a system to play the sound of dogs barking when the bear returned from brief forays.

Eventually, Mr. Johnson got in touch with the Bear League, a group based in the Lake Tahoe area, which helped him install electrified mats that give bears a little jolt to teach them to stay away.

The bear never came back.

Ann Bryant, who helped start the Bear League some 30 years ago, said that many Southern Californians were in similar straits.

“There are certain things they have to do, and there are certain things they cannot do, in order to live in bear country,” she said. Bear-safe garbage cans are mandatory in many Lake-Tahoe-area communities, so that trash day does not become a buffet. Businesses make the electrified mats that keep bears from denning in crawl spaces.

Bears, she said, should not be harmed because of “human error and human negligence.”

The stakes for the animals can be life or death.

This year, after a bear known as Blondie injured a woman who was walking her dog in Monrovia, state wildlife officials euthanized the bear, orphaning her cubs. Mr. Gordon and other residents hosted a vigil.

Arjun Dheer, the California Department of Fish and Wildlife’s black bear research coordinator, said that Southern California’s population had a complicated history: In 1933, a car salesman trucked a couple dozen from the Yosemite National Park area to the San Gabriel and San Bernardino Mountains. Park staff had been throwing garbage into “bear pits” to lure the animals to tourist areas. The businessman had the idea that the bears could become a similar draw farther south.

Dr. Dheer said that many of the estimated 2,000 bears in Southern California were related to those first 27 bears.

They are resilient, with an adaptable diet and flexibility in climes they can inhabit, he said. But the impulse to anthropomorphize bears by naming them and chronicling their antics risks encouraging human misbehavior. People who don’t know better may leave food out in hopes of attracting bears or fail to secure their homes and cars.

That, in turn, can make the animals and their offspring more dependent on human food sources, and thus more aggressive. This often ends poorly.

“We want to keep bears wild,” Dr. Dheer said. “A fed bear is a dead bear.”

John Harabedian, a state lawmaker who grew up in Sierra Madre, said he proposed legislation last year that would have directed the Department of Fish and Wildlife to more closely study Southern California’s bear population. It didn’t pass, largely because of the cost, but he plans to introduce similar legislation again.

Residents, he said, have backed a wide range of solutions.

“Folks have called for the outright euthanization of all of them,” he said. Others don’t believe that they should even be relocated, “because, in their view, the bears were here first.”

Mr. Gordon, the bear fan from Monrovia, said that he was skeptical of the government’s priorities and that tagging bears just to monitor them seemed unnecessary.

“I don’t think we should be disturbing the bear’s normal life,” he said, “just because it stepped one paw into private property.”

item.title: One School District’s Fight Against Trump’s Anti-Transgender Push
item.description:
Rob Stein had been interim school superintendent in Jefferson County, Colo., for 22 days when he sued the Trump administration this summer over demands to change their transgender-inclusive policies.

Dr. Stein and other district officials say they had no choice. The cash-strapped district, Jeffco Public Schools, risked losing all $50 million of its federal funding for school meals and special education if they refused. But if they acquiesced, they concluded, they would violate state laws that protect transgender students from discrimination.

“This has been just an enormous distraction,” Dr. Stein said in an interview from the district’s foothill-framed headquarters. “It has added a lot of stress to the system and to the kids who are being targeted here.”

What the district cast as a practical decision is viewed as a rare counterstrike from public schools, universities and hospitals in support of a transgender rights movement that has been on its heels under President Trump after a decade of hard-fought successes in school board rooms and courts.

Z Williams, an advocate for transgender rights and co-director of the Bread and Roses Legal Center in Denver, said most institutions facing pressure have opted for “voluntary capitulation.”

Some schools targeted by the Trump administration have agreed to settlements or changed their policies based on Mr. Trump’s executive orders that forbid the government from recognizing gender identity instead of biological sex, barred transgender athletes in female sports and rolled back prior administrative guidance that sex-discrimination laws protected gender identity.

“I’m just incredibly proud of this school board,” Z Williams said. “Trans people are being more and more villainized and more and more marginalized. So it’s really impressive for Jeffco to fight on these issues.”

The dispute has thrust the school district into the center of the mushrooming culture war that Mr. Trump has led against transgender Americans. It encapsulates virtually every flashpoint of the political struggle between gender identity and biological sex that has become central to Mr. Trump’s effort to reassert conservative social values into public schools and universities.

The legal battle has also put a spotlight on an impossible squeeze facing educators across the country. Caught between state laws or court orders protecting transgender students and the executive decrees from the White House aimed at undercutting those safeguards, Jeffco is testing the limits of federal pressure versus local governance.

The Education Department, where Linda McMahon, the education secretary, received a summons in the lawsuit on Aug. 13, has not yet filed its formal response with the court. In a statement, a spokeswoman said the agency had referred the case to the Justice Department because the district had “taken no steps to protect women and girls.”

The investigation into Jeffco is one of more than five dozen the administration has opened into school districts and universities since 2025 over potential violations of anti-discrimination protections for female students, widely known as Title IX. The administration argues that allowing those assigned as male at birth access to girls’ sports teams and bathrooms violates Title IX and risks distressing girls.

In March, the administration announced that Jeffco had violated federal nondiscrimination laws by allowing students access to restrooms, locker rooms and sports teams based on their gender identity instead of biological sex. A key data point was that 61 boys were participating on girls’ athletic teams. The figure startled even district officials, mostly because, they said, there were no transgender girls competing on girls’ teams.

The district said the Trump administration had misinterpreted the information. Though the records show male participants on girls’ teams, they were team managers and mascots, not athletes. District officials said the federal government also may have confused a cross-country roster in which the same coach oversees separate programs for boys and girls.

Asked about the discrepancy, an Education Department spokesperson repeated that federal investigators determined male participants had “at least 61 roster spots on girls’ sports teams.”

To lead its defense in court, the district has enlisted the law firm of Jack Smith, the former special counsel who directed a pair of criminal investigations against Mr. Trump resulting in grand jury indictments. The firm also represents other districts facing similar investigations, including Shawnee Mission, Kan.; Montgomery County, Md.; and Fairfax County, Va.

The Jeffco lawsuit accuses the administration of failing to follow proper procedures in threatening the funding cuts, and of misinterpreting Title IX to mean that schools must separate students by their biological sex in restrooms and athletic facilities.

“No court has so held,” according to the lawsuit, “no properly issued regulations so require, and the Supreme Court expressly left that question open.”

Federal laws typically override conflicting state statutes, but the district argues that state law outweighs White House decrees. The Colorado Anti-Discrimination Act, first enacted in 1957, was updated in 2007 and in the years since to extend protections to transgender people.

The dispute has drawn key Washington figures to Colorado. Early last month, Harmeet Dhillon, the government’s top civil rights lawyer, was the keynote speaker at a fund-raiser for Jeffco Kids First, a local parents’ rights group. The group has filed multiple complaints with the federal government about the school district’s gender policies since last year, Lindsay Datko, the head of Jeffco Kids First, said in an interview.

During the event, held in a hotel ballroom across the street from the school district offices, Ms. Dhillon gave credit to Jeffco Kids First and other conservative-leaning parent groups, which the administration has increasingly relied on to identify targets for civil rights investigations.

“Passionate community members — like all of you in this room — are part of the reason why this Department of Justice, perhaps for the first time ever, is taking the side of parents as vigorously as you’re seeing in this administration,” she said.

A Justice Department spokeswoman said that Ms. Dhillon left before fund-raising activities started and that her appearance was approved by the agency’s ethics team.

Ms. Datko, a former teacher with four children enrolled in JeffCo schools, said she formed Jeffco Kids First in 2020 in response to restrictions from the Covid-19 pandemic. The group’s attention has since turned to other issues, including gender policies, which she said had become so expansive that they were hurting the broader student body.

“If these policies are meant to give equal opportunities to everyone, isn’t it now doing the opposite?” she said. “Policies that accommodate a transgender child can accommodate other children as well.”

At a back-to-school meeting in August with school principals and other senior staff, district officials were walked through recent changes about how to talk with students about gender identity. Teachers, for example, no longer give students surveys that ask if it’s OK to use their pronouns when teachers call home.

Dr. Stein, the interim superintendent, said the language was aimed at being “more mindful” to concerns in the community while balancing student needs. “We also don’t want to squelch inquiry and suppress kids as they develop their own means of expression,” he said.

But that expression can, at times, be more difficult at home than at school for students like Olie Parlett, 14, who came out as nonbinary two years ago to his mother and stepfather, but feared their biological father’s reaction.

The private turmoil in their household over gender identity was thrust into the public square when Olie’s father, Dustin Gonzalez, stood at the lectern of a school board meeting last year and blamed district policies for his lack of awareness about his child’s preferred name and pronouns. Mr. Gonzalez had not been part of meetings about the changes with Olie and their mother, Bee Parlett, with a school counselor.

The moment went viral on social media as Elon Musk, and conservative influencers reposted the clip to suggest woke local school districts were brainwashing the nation’s children.

Mr. Gonzalez said in an interview that he had lost some of his custody rights during the past year, and had been estranged from his oldest child since May. He has pulled his two younger children, both from his second marriage, out of public schools and warned fellow parents to “be as involved as humanly possible” with the children.

Mr. Gonzalez criticized the county for suing the government. “This all started with them, all of it,” he said.

Sitting in a diner, picking at a breakfast of eggs and toast, Olie spoke about the series of extraordinary highs and lows already logged on their short journey, including feeling targeted and dismissed by the president of the United States. They also recalled the strict science teacher known to inspire fear in students who showed them unexpected empathy.

But Olie appeared torn about whether lawsuits would help change any minds about gender identity issues.

“People hate what they don’t understand,” Olie said. “But if they would just hang out with someone who is trans or go to a drag show, they would see the healing joy, and in about 10 minutes their preconceived notions will not be there.”

item.title: As War Grinds On, Trump Relishes Renovation Projects
item.description:
Howard Lutnick, President Trump’s billionaire commerce secretary, was holding court before reporters outside a Washington courthouse recently when he acknowledged what had become readily apparent inside the White House.

As the war with Iran grinds on, Mr. Trump finds reprieve by focusing on the minutia of an endeavor much more within his grasp: renovating Washington with ornate projects.

“He loves to build,” Mr. Lutnick said, shortly before an emergency hearing about Mr. Trump’s desire to rename the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts in his own honor. Mr. Lutnick added: “This is what he enjoys. So late at night, 11 o’clock at night, he calls me and wants to talk about things he’s building, because it’s fun for him.”

“If you sat with him, would you have a nice chat with him? No, you’d ask him about Iran, then you’d ask him about this, then you’d ask him about that,” he noted. “Everybody does that. And the one thing he likes to do during the week is construction.”

As the United States appears mired in another intractable conflict in the Middle East, Mr. Trump has basked in the momentum he has on the half-dozen makeover projects he has set in motion throughout the capital.

The Supreme Court gave him a green light to race forward with construction of the White House ballroom. The administration said it planned to start excavation work for a 250-foot-tall triumphal arch near Arlington National Cemetery even before a federal review panel had approved the project. The Kennedy Center board, stocked with the president’s loyalists, voted to add Mr. Trump’s name below the main sign on the building, and abruptly removed a large outdoor sculpture, “Blue,” from the grounds.

Mr. Trump’s primary background is not in government or finance, but in construction and real estate. In New York City, he often lamented the never-ending series of zoning regulations, permits and community-level approvals needed to get projects built.

Making changes to a project there requires hours of sitting in community meetings listening to complaints from residents, and getting sign-off from city officials. Projects like helipads, Mr. Trump has complained, are next-to-impossible to get approved. But in his second term as president, he said, he realized he could barrel over many of those impediments. He stocked review panels with White House appointees. Court challenges have failed to keep pace with the administration’s rapid construction. He can finally just have fun.

“You mean I can actually do something that I really want?” Mr. Trump told a room full of donors to his White House ballroom last year, describing what it had been like overseeing construction projects as president.

“‘You’re the president of the United States. You can do anything you want,’” Mr. Trump has said he has been told.

In a statement, a White House spokesman, Davis Ingle, said, “President Trump can walk and chew gum at the same time. As a result, the Trump Administration continues to deliver on the president’s campaign promises.”

“Thanks to the Builder-in-Chief, no other president has done more to beautify our nation’s interior than President Trump,” he added.

His breakneck makeover efforts in Washington have illustrated the administration’s willingness to sidestep laws and intimidate critics.

Mr. Trump abruptly tore down the White House’s historic East Wing without seeking approval from Congress, after saying that the ballroom would be next to the older structure but would not touch it. He constructed an imposing White House helipad also without going through any review process. And the administration has announced that it is moving ahead with his giant arch before the review process is complete. (The Justice Department on Friday said in a court filing that the government just planned to do an archaeological excavation of the site necessary for a historic review, and that no final decision had been made.)

Mr. Trump’s remaking of the Reflecting Pool near the Lincoln Memorial began as another such adventure in speed, with the president telling people he brought in his “pool guy” to fix leaks and damage to the decades-old site. Instead, it became a symbol of dysfunction, as the new coating peeled. The president blamed “vandals,” without providing evidence. Jeanine Pirro, the U.S. attorney in Washington, vowed to aggressively prosecute a former Olympian accused of the crime, only to have to reverse herself when the case fell apart.

The tab for the various construction projects that Mr. Trump has launched come with a potential cost of as much as $1 billion, much of it at taxpayer expense. Nearly two-thirds of Americans have a negative view of his three main projects, according to a Washington Post/Ipsos poll taken in July.

In a White House where one meeting often rolls into another, Mr. Trump’s visits with old friends or administration officials have invariably collided with his many planning sessions for his beautification and building projects, from the remodeling of a golf course along the Potomac River to what some have referred to as the “Arc de Trump.”

He is at his most animated, aides and visitors to the White House say, when he is showing off the designs for the ballroom, boasting about the size of the columns and their designs, or taking officials on tours of the White House to show off where he has gilded the interiors. His personal touch has been quite literal: He has used super glue to affix gold pieces onto the walls and the Oval Office mantle, among other places.

The White House has argued that the new ballroom is necessary to accommodate events for visiting dignitaries, and for national security reasons, as it is being built over an emergency operations bunker.

But Mr. Trump also appears determined to erect edifices that cannot be torn down after he is gone. He was enraged when his name was pulled down from residential buildings in New York City in protest after his first divisive political campaign in 2016, according to people close to him. Properties in other countries, including in Canada, followed suit.

Other presidents have had monuments built in their honor by future generations. There is no tradition in the United States of presidents naming buildings for themselves. Mr. Trump does not appear to expect anything like that will happen unless he builds the structures himself.

“Nobody will do it once I’m gone,” he recently told New York Magazine. “When I leave here, nobody will.”

It is a belief that Mr. Trump has long held. In 1980, he described to The New York Times his experience attending the opening of the Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge connecting Brooklyn to Staten Island, alongside his developer father, Fred. What stuck with him: The man who designed the historic suspension bridge was never acknowledged by name during the event.

“I realized then and there that if you let people treat you how they want, you’ll be made a fool,” Mr. Trump said. “I realized then and there something I would never forget: I don’t want to be made anybody’s sucker.”

In addition to his weekend golf sessions, overseeing construction is what the president actually likes to do. The happiest hours of his week in the first months of his second term were when he would work on his redesign of the Rose Garden, or pluck portraits and gold items from the White House curator’s collection to augment his style in the Oval Office, aides said.

“I’m a really good builder,” he told reporters in May, while taking them on a tour of the White House ballroom construction. “The thing I do best in life is build.”

item.title: Fact-Checking Midterm Ads Referring to Jeffrey Epstein
item.description:
The fallout over the convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and his crimes has emerged as a major issue in the midterm elections.

Candidates have hammered their opponents over whether they pushed to release the investigative files related to Mr. Epstein, and over their connections to donors and supporters associated with him. Over and over, they have issued a common refrain: They are running against the “Epstein class.”

The New York Times identified at least 35 congressional races with TV or digital ads that mentioned “Epstein” between January 2026 and the end of August, according to an analysis of data from AdImpact, a media tracking firm. The stream of ads remained steady through the summer.

In trying to tie their opponents to the disgraced financier, some ads have omitted context or promoted weak links to Mr. Epstein. Here’s a look.

Until last November, Republicans in Congress were torn between voters pressing for the release of the Epstein files, and President Trump’s monthslong resistance to doing so.

More than a dozen Democratic candidates and their allies in House and Senate races highlighted votes by Republican rivals opposing efforts in the spring and summer of 2025 to release the Epstein files.

It is true that all but nine House Republicans voted in July 2025 against a procedural move to release the files (those nine members did not vote at all), and all but two Senate Republicans voted in September 2025 against an amendment to release the files. Republican members of the Rules Committee, which controls the pathway to bringing a bill to the House floor for a vote, stymied efforts to force the issue several times.

But the attack ads all omit that Republicans reversed their positions once Mr. Trump bowed to pressure last November. A measure to release the files passed by unanimous consent in the Senate and nearly unanimously in the House.

In Georgia, an ad from the campaign of Senator Jon Ossoff, a Democrat, noted that his Republican opponent, Representative Mike Collins, “voted against releasing the Epstein files,” referring to that vote in July. Another campaign video added that Mr. Collins “even admitted Trump was in the files.”

That was a misleading reference to comments Mr. Collins made at a Republican Party event last August. Asked whether he believed Mr. Trump was in the Epstein files, Mr. Collins responded, “I’m sure he’s in there because he’s the one who was telling the F.B.I. about it.” (Mr. Collins’s comment was not accurate, either. The files contain tens of thousands of references to Mr. Trump, and they include mentions in news articles and in salacious and unverified tips.)

Meyer Siegfried, a spokesman for the Collins campaign, said Mr. Ossoff was “a shameless hypocrite” given that his campaign had received contributions from Reid Hoffman, the billionaire co-founder of LinkedIn who also corresponded with Mr. Epstein and visited his island at least once.

In Florida, an ad from Gay Valimont, a Democratic candidate for a House seat, accuses Representative Jimmy Patronis, a Republican, of calling “investigating Jeffrey Epstein a waste of his time.”

That is not quite what Mr. Patronis said. Appearing on local radio in July 2025, he asserted that he had “no problem getting everything all released.” But he expressed frustration that the issue had “created an impasse for us getting things done.”

Mr. Epstein’s wide-ranging connections with powerful people have led to recriminations in finance, politics, academia and entertainment. Political donations from those people are now fodder for attack ads.

In the Senate race in Ohio, both candidates traded attacks highlighting campaign contributions from donors with ties to Mr. Epstein.

Sherrod Brown, a former Democratic senator who is mounting a comeback campaign, has run at least eight different ads highlighting donations that Senator Jon Husted, a Republican, received from Leslie Wexner, a retail billionaire from Ohio who employed Mr. Epstein as his financial manager for decades and was identified in one exchange in 2019 among federal agents as a potential “co-conspirator.” (A legal representative for Mr. Wexner told The Times in 2025 that he was not a target of the federal investigation or considered a co-conspirator, and that Mr. Wexner had provided investigators with background information.)

“Husted took more money from Jeffrey Epstein’s co-conspirators than anyone else in Washington and then voted to keep the Epstein files secret,” one ad claims.

Like all but two other Senate Republicans, Mr. Husted voted against releasing the Epstein files in September 2025, but reversed his position last November.

Mr. Wexner has donated more than $116,000 to Mr. Husted’s state and federal campaigns since 2001. Mr. Husted’s team does not dispute that figure, which includes contributions made to the campaign of Gov. Mike DeWine of Ohio, a Republican, while Mr. Husted was his running mate.

Amy Natoce, a spokeswoman for Mr. Husted’s campaign, said that it had donated all available funds, totaling $34,300, to an anti-human trafficking charity. Donations from Mr. Wexner in past election cycles were spent and no longer accessible, she said.

Since 2001, Mr. Wexner has contributed more than $3 million to federal campaign coffers, the vast majority to Republicans, particularly in his home state of Ohio. Several other candidates and their affiliated political action committees received far more money than Mr. Husted, including Jeb Bush (more than $500,000) and Rob Portman (more than $300,000). None are currently in office.

In response, Mr. Husted has broadcast an ad calling Mr. Brown a liar, accusing him of accepting “a hundred grand from Epstein associates.”

The Husted campaign cited more than a dozen donors with varying degrees of associations to Mr. Epstein. Ms. Natoce questioned why, unlike the Husted campaign, the Brown campaign had not donated the contributions.

The donors include people with direct links to Mr. Epstein, such as Larry Summers, a former president of Harvard who routinely corresponded withMr. Epstein; Mr. Hoffman; Barry Diller, a Hollywood magnate who once visited Mr. Epstein’s island; and several people who exchanged emails with Mr. Epstein or Ghislaine Maxwell, a longtime associate of Mr. Epstein’s who was convicted in 2021 for facilitating sexual abuse.

But others had more tenuous or virtually nonexistent ties, including: Mr. Wexner’s wife, Abigail Wexner; Laurene Powell Jobs, the widow of the Apple co-founder Steve Jobs; and the billionaire financier George Soros, who has no known links to Mr. Epstein.

In a few races, campaigns have focused on their opponents’ or their fund-raisers’ more direct links to Mr. Epstein.

In the Nebraska Senate race, Senator Pete Ricketts, a Republican, ran at least four different ads attacking Dan Osborn, an independent, for fund-raising with an “Epstein associate” named Dana Chasin.

“Chasin allegedly transported victims to Epstein’s home,” one ad claims. “Even after that information was public, Osborn continued to raise money with Chasin, until he got caught.”

Mr. Chasin, a Democratic operative and donor, gave $3,300 to Mr. Osborn’s campaign in March 2024. His name appeared in files that were released on Jan. 30, 2026, in a March 2024 email from a lawyer representing a woman who said that she had been sexually abused by a billionaire investor associated with Mr. Epstein. The lawyer, who later withdrew from the case, wrote that a person whose name is redacted flew on Mr. Chasin’s “small prop plane” to Mr. Epstein’s townhouse. (Mr. Chasin denied the allegations and told Politico that he had never owned or rented a prop plane.)

Mr. Osborn had been scheduled to attend a fund-raiser on Feb. 10 co-hosted by Mr. Chasin. But after Politico highlighted the email, he canceled the gathering. The Daily Wire, a conservative publication, also reported that a link to the canceled fund-raiser was still soliciting donations. The Osborn campaign took it down in late February.

Asked about the donation and the fund-raiser, Mr. Osborn said on Facebook in March that Mr. Chasin’s connection to Mr. Epstein “wasn’t widely known at that point” and that he “immediately” canceled the fund-raiser upon learning of it. He added that he had given Mr. Chasin’s $3,300 to a charity that supports sexual abuse victims.

The Osborn campaign said the ads were “laughable,” and noted Mr. Ricketts’ vote against releasing the Epstein files in September 2025. In a statement, the Ricketts campaign questioned why Mr. Osborn had not donated any contributions raised in association with Mr. Chasin’s canceled fund-raiser.

In the Senate race in New Hampshire, Representative Chris Pappas, a Democrat, has zeroed in on a mention of his Republican rival, the former senator John E. Sununu, in the Epstein files.

“John Sununu denied that his name appears in the Epstein files and denied ever attending an elite event in Doha, Qatar, that Jeffrey Epstein used for networking,” one Facebook ad from the Pappas campaign reads. “The receipts prove otherwise. And separate reporting shows Sununu’s campaign has accepted contributions from billionaires with ties to Epstein.”

Mr. Pappas is correct that Mr. Sununu falsely denied attending the World Economic Forum in Doha in 2010. It is also true that Mr. Sununu’s name appears in the Epstein files. But the mention is brief, and it is unclear whether that reference was actually to Mr. Sununu or to his father.

In an email exchange that year, Boris Nikolic, a Gates Foundation adviser, asked Mr. Epstein if there was anyone he should meet at the event. Mr. Epstein mentioned Mr. Sununu, saying he had “good stories.”

Mr. Nikolic and Mr. Epstein did not clarify which John Sununu: John E. Sununu, the former senator, or John H. Sununu, his father who was the governor of New Hampshire and a former chief of staff to President George H.W. Bush. There is also no record in the files of Mr. Sununu meeting with Mr. Nikolic or Mr. Epstein at the event, which more than 450 people attended.

Mike Schrimpf, a spokesman for the Sununu campaign, called the ad “disgusting,” and said that neither Mr. Sununu nor his father “ever met or communicated in any way with Boris Nikolic or Jeffrey Epstein.”

item.title: As Gas Prices Soar, These Drivers Squeeze Every Mile From Every Gallon
item.description:
When a traffic light turns green, Dan Kroushl is unlikely to be the first driver out of the gate. He won’t floor the gas pedal, and he never drives over the speed limit.

Instead, he eases forward by lightly pressing the accelerator, and the moment he sees a yellow light, he gently taps the brakes.

These techniques and others make Mr. Kroushl, 61, a so-called hypermiler, a driver who squeezes as many miles as possible out of each gallon of gas. And after a summer of soaring gas prices driven by the war in Iran, hypermilers like Mr. Kroushl say their strategies can help drivers who are feeling pinched at the pump make the most of every gallon.

“People think when they are pumping gas: I can’t do anything about it,” Bradlee Fons, 74, a fellow hypermiler, said of the increased gas prices. “I tell them, ‘You’re in total control.’ People can control their fuel costs.”

Hypermilers mostly aim to maximize fuel efficiency by driving smoothly, without hard stops or starts. But sometimes they employ more extreme measures, like not using air conditioning or removing a vehicle’s interior door panels to reduce its weight.

It’s both a lifestyle choice and a way to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, the hypermilers say, but they think some of their strategies could be useful to regular, everyday drivers looking to save on fillups.

Gas prices have risen sharply since the United States and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. 28, freezing the flow of energy from the Persian Gulf. As fighting in Iran intensified last week, diesel fuel prices hit a record high in the United States, with gas prices up nearly 40 percent, according to the AAA motor club.

As of Sunday, regular gas costs an average of $4.14 per gallon, though prices vary in different states. According to AAA, it is the highest price for a gallon of regular gas on Labor Day weekend, though that does not account for inflation.

With a few tweaks, Mr. Fons said, drivers can easily save 30 percent or more on their gas bill.

“Drivers do not have to be at the mercy of the government, the high gas prices or anything else,” he said. “They have options.”

The 2017 Toyota Prius that Mr. Fons drives in his home in Jackson, Wis., just north of Milwaukee, is estimated to achieve 52 miles per gallon, according to its official E.P.A. rating. But, Mr. Fons said, he gets 83.2 miles per gallon by driving with fuel economy in mind.

Mr. Fons, who started a nonprofit organization called Drive Smart Wisconsin, keeps a list of simple techniques that he said any driver can use to save money on gas. At the top of the list is “nonaggressive driving,” which he defined as moving smoothly and purposefully. Other strategies include completing multiple errands in one trip so the car does not use extra fuel to warm up, and keeping up with vehicle maintenance.

Most cars are at peak fuel efficiency between 45 and 65 miles per hour. Hypermilers recommend staying in that range and not going over the speed limit on the highway. Driving faster causes the vehicle’s drag to increase, reducing fuel mileage at an exponential rate.

Hypermilers also avoid unnecessary braking, which eats up fuel, and they accelerate slowly when starting from a complete stop. They anticipate slowdowns ahead.

“You work the gas so you’re barely holding the speed you want to hold,” explained Bruce Gregersen, 79, a hypermiler who lives in St. Cloud, Minn. “It takes a little more concentration, but once you get used to it, you’ll do it automatically.”

Hybrid cars, which combine a traditional gasoline-powered engine with one or more electric motors and a battery pack, offer greater fuel efficiency and are the vehicle of choice for many hypermilers.

Bob Winger, 71, a Williamsburg, Va., resident, is part of a group of hypermile enthusiasts who have set multiple world records for fuel efficiency, including one for the lowest consumption of fuel in a non-hybrid vehicle driving through all 48 contiguous states. Mr. Winger said they had set that record by using techniques such as “ridge riding,” in which the passenger-side wheel moves along the white paint stripe on a highway because the friction is lower there than on the asphalt.

Such extremes are not necessary unless one is trying to set a world record, Mr. Winger said. Instead, he said, drivers can achieve greater mileage by doing simple things like making sure their tires are properly inflated, which helps decrease resistance. Using full synthetic oil in the engine reduces friction within the engine, he added.

“You don’t have to do crazy stuff,” he said. “Just driving conservatively, you can save without really pulling out all the tools in the toolbox.”

Susan C. Beachy and Georgia Gee contributed research.

item.title: Trump Floats Renaming New Mexico as ‘New America,’ Prompting Pushback
item.description:
President Trump appeared to suggest on Sunday that New Mexico should be renamed “New America,” prompting swift backlash from the state’s Democratic leaders over his latest effort to put an American stamp on geographic names.

On social media, Mr. Trump shared an image of a map of New Mexico with the word “Mexico” crossed out with a red X and replaced with “America.” The White House re-shared the image shortly after on its official X account.

The president posted again several hours later, with what appeared to be an A.I. video of him placing a label with the word “America” over “Mexico” on a “Welcome to New Mexico” road sign.

Mr. Trump frequently uses social media to troll his perceived adversaries. His posts quickly drew criticism from officials in New Mexico, a Democratic-led state.

“New Mexico’s name isn’t up for debate — it’s been ours since before the United States existed,” Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham wrote on social media.

Representative Melanie Stansbury was more blunt: “Oh hell no!” she wrote on X, adding, “Our state’s name carries generations of history, culture, and family — and it belongs to us.”

The origins of New Mexico’s name predate the founding of the United States. In the 16th century, Mexicans called the territory north and west of the Rio Grande “New Mexico,” according to the Bureau of Indian Affairs.

The state’s name is also written into Article 1 of its Constitution: “The name of this state is New Mexico, and its boundaries are as follows,” the first page reads.

New Mexico’s two Democratic senators also pushed back on Mr. Trump’s post. “Three things I will always call by their actual names …” Senator Martin Heinrich wrote on X, before listing the Gulf of Mexico, Lake Ontario and New Mexico.

On the day Mr. Trump returned to office last year, he signed an executive order directing the federal government to rename the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America. The name “has a beautiful ring,” the president said that month.

Last month, amid an escalating trade fight with Canada, Mr. Trump signed another executive order to change the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America. Days before signing the order, the president had posted an image of a map with Lake Ontario crossed out with a red X, as well as an A.I. video of himself replacing a Lake Ontario sign with “Lake America.”

Those executive orders, however, dealt with geographic features, not the legal name of a state. The changes were carried out through the federal Geographic Names Information System and apply only to federal usage, including on maps and documents, but they do not bind state and local governments or private mapmakers.

Rhode Island offers a recent example of how different the process for changing the legal name of a state can be. In June 2020, amid nationwide protests over systemic racism after the killing of George Floyd, the state moved to drop “and Providence Plantations” from its formal name. Gov. Gina Raimondo, a Democrat, ordered the phrase be removed from executive-branch documents and websites while acknowledging that changing the state’s official name required voters to amend the Rhode Island Constitution. Voters approved the change that fall.
