item.title: Trump’s Trade War Is Shaping the Fight for Congress
item.description:
Colorado’s annual state fair in historic Pueblo is a celebration of the state’s deep farming and ranching roots and agriculture’s significant contribution to the state economy, a reality sometimes lost in the public focus on the region’s stunning mountain vistas, adventurous outdoor sports and glitzy ski towns.

This year, the party was a bit muted.

Colorado’s farmers and ranchers are struggling against factors beyond their control, with higher costs for fuel and fertilizer resulting from President Trump’s decision to wage a trade war featuring steep tariffs and an actual war against Iran. In a bid to lower meat prices last month, the president also agreed to allow cheaper beef imports to compete with domestic cattle producers who were finally turning the corner after difficult years.

“For the first time, our cow-calf producers are making a living and being able to sell their calves at a reasonable price,” said Erin Spaur, the executive vice president of the Colorado Cattlemen’s Association, as youngsters showed off their prize hogs in the fair’s livestock exhibition hall. “We believe in fair trade, but we don’t believe this is the best avenue forward,” she said of the administration’s move to temporarily lift duties on beef.

The economic anxieties of these generally conservative Coloradans — as well as voters in similar communities throughout the country buffeted by Mr. Trump’s whipsawing trade decisions — are one reason Democrats are hopeful about their chances of winning control of Congress in November. The party is optimistic about picking up at least one seat in Colorado, and potentially more as the president’s popularity sinks.

Two House Republicans fighting to hold onto their jobs have responded with divergent strategies — one stressing his opposition to Mr. Trump’s moves and the other hugging him tightly — in a state where the president has grown more unpopular.

In the state’s Third District, which sprawls across almost its entire western half, Representative Jeff Hurd, a first-term Republican, has leaned into his differences with Mr. Trump. Earlier this year, the president unendorsed and then re-endorsed Mr. Hurd, who broke with him and voted in February to end his tariffs on Canada.

“I value the relationship that I have with the president, with the administration, and I support his goals,” Mr. Hurd said during an interview after a fair luncheon recognizing families that have owned their ranches for at least a century. “But at the end of the day, Congress has a role under Article I, Section 8 of the Constitution,” he added, referring to the portion that gives the legislative branch power to regulate trade, “and also, I have a duty to serve the people that elected me.”

In the more competitive Eighth Congressional District immediately north of Denver, with its mix of economically pressed blue-collar workers and ranchers, Representative Gabe Evans, another first-term Republican, has instead emphasized his allegiance to the president. He has been a reliable supporter of Mr. Trump’s tariff policy and blames Democrats, including his state’s governor, Jared Polis, for regulatory restrictions he argues have pushed up fuel prices and contributed to high costs.

“There are national drivers, but here in the state of Colorado, the state has declared war on oil and gas,” Mr. Evans said as he accepted an endorsement from the U.S. Chamber of Commerce at a Mexican restaurant on his district’s border with Denver. “People know that Jared Polis and his Democrats have wrecked this state. They have uniquely wrecked my district, which is based on oil, gas and ag.”

It is a high-stakes strategy in a state where Mr. Trump has grown unpopular after targeting Colorado for its resistance to some of his policies, as well as the jailing of a former county elections official and 2020 election denier before Mr. Polis reduced her sentence under White House pressure. Tariff and trade issues could be decisive not just here in the Rocky Mountains, but also in marquee contests for the Senate in Maine, Michigan, Alaska, New Hampshire and Ohio, as well as competitive House races across the Midwest.

Underscoring the potential for conservative backlash, Senator Mike Rounds, Republican of South Dakota, said ranchers feel like Mr. Trump “pulled the rug right out from underneath” them. “They’re hurt. I mean, they feel like they’ve been let down,” Mr. Rounds told reporters at the Capitol last week.

In Colorado, Mr. Evans is being challenged by Manny Rutinel, a 31-year-old state representative who emphasizes his family’s economic struggles as he was growing up — noting that he used to sell his blood plasma to help pay the bills.

As he mingled with supporters at the popular Tacos Los Viejones Mexican street food stand across from a gas station that showed diesel selling at nearly $5.50 a gallon, Mr. Rutinel said Mr. Evans’s constituents deserved a change given the congressman’s support of White House policies making their lives unaffordable.

“Tariffs are the reason why our grocery prices are soaring at the moment, and they are also at the same time kicking the teeth of our farmers and ranchers and putting their livelihoods at risk,” Mr. Rutinel said. “And Gabe Evans has been in lock step with Donald Trump in enabling these policies that are making life impossible in America.”

The concentration of cattle ranchers in the district has added a twist to the race: Mr. Evans likes to note that, in Mr. Rutinel’s younger days, he was a very public vegan and animal rights activist.

“We have my opponent, who has called for vice taxes on meat, dairy and eggs and says that we have to transition away from animal agriculture and everyone has to eat tofu,” Mr. Evans said. “That doesn’t sell in this district.”

Mr. Rutinel, who very noticeably ate carne asada at the street food stand for the cameras of a local Hispanic food influencer, dismissed the criticism as irrelevant and said his vegan days were behind him.

“The truth is Coloradans don’t care what’s on my plate,” he said in an interview. “They care about being able to afford what is on theirs.”

In the Third District, the Democrat Dwayne Romero, a former Aspen city councilman, West Point graduate and decorated military veteran who is challenging Mr. Hurd, said a single vote against Mr. Trump’s tariff policies hardly makes a maverick of his opponent.

“One alternative vote doesn’t make the man,” said Mr. Romero, the former state director of economic development who has served on multiple local boards. “Doesn’t make the backbone. Doesn’t make the position of defending his constituents. It is almost a throwaway.”

He said Mr. Hurd had been aligned with Mr. Trump on almost every issue, including a major tax and policy measure that included health care and safety net cuts, and that both the congressman and the president have retreated from pledges to lower costs and avoid drawn-out military conflicts. The push to import cheaper beef is just the latest economic weight placed on ranchers by the administration, he said.

“It is really just putting a finger in the eye of our ranching community to import beef at a discounted price just to relieve some of the expense,” Mr. Romero said. “It really is salt in the wound.”

Mr. Hurd conceded that ranchers in the district were alarmed by the White House policy coming after they thought they had weathered the worst: contending with drought, wildfires and the voter-mandated reintroduction of wolves to the mountains. He said he believed those ranchers recognized that he would do what he can to back them.

“The people that I represent, at the end of the day, I trust them,” Mr. Hurd said. “I trust them to see me as somebody who reflects their values.”

As Democrats try to take over these districts, that is one of their chief obstacles: persuading Republican-leaning voters that it is time to make a change.

Jake Bachman, a coffee shop owner and rancher from Johnstown, whose son, Gavin, was showing his lambs at the fair, said the economic pressures were formidable, but he was still backing Mr. Evans over the Democrat.

“We are getting squeezed,” he said. “Obviously, costs across the board are going up. Sometimes it is like when there’s a flood: You are doing the best you can to try to stop some of it, even though you may not be able to stop all of it. That’s what it feels like.”

item.title: Why Amy Klobuchar Wants to Run a State Beleaguered by Trump
item.description:
On a sweltering summer morning, Senator Amy Klobuchar was making small talk with merchants at the St. Paul farmer’s market when a cheesemaker expressed a sentiment that has kept coming up as Ms. Klobuchar campaigns for governor.

“We’re going to miss you in Washington,” the cheesemaker, Brenda Carlson, told the senator while bagging a piece of Tilsit.

Ms. Klobuchar acknowledged having mixed feelings about leaving her seat as the chamber’s third highest-ranking Democrat. “But we need to get this sorted out,” she said, frowning slightly.

By this, Ms. Klobuchar meant the current condition of Minnesota, which has become a punching bag in the Trump administration’s quest to portray Democratic-run states and cities as hopelessly dysfunctional.

As she gears up for what could be the capstone of a decades-long political career, Ms. Klobuchar is pitching herself as uniquely qualified to clean up the messes at home and reset the state’s poisonous relationship with the White House.

Her reputation makes the case, supporters say: She is known as both a hard-charging workaholic who scrutinizes program details to a fault and a centrist with allies on both sides of the aisle in Washington, including in the Trump administration.

But both qualities could also cause friction. Minnesota agencies are bracing for turbulence as Ms. Klobuchar vows to audit every state program. And many residents remain shell shocked from the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown early this year, which paralyzed the Twin Cities for weeks and left two U.S. citizens dead.

When it comes to relations with the president, some residents say they want a fighter in the governor’s office, not a conciliator.

Nekima Levy Armstrong, a civil rights lawyer who is facing trial over her role organizing an anti-ICE protest at a church, said Ms. Klobuchar did not speak out stridently enough about the wintertime deportation campaign.

“Many of us felt abandoned by our elected officials during Operation Metro Surge,” Ms. Levy Armstrong said. “We felt abandoned by Amy Klobuchar in particular.”

In an interview, Ms. Klobuchar said she was “as angry about some of the things Trump has done as anyone.”

“But I have decided that I’m going to get us to a higher place and not act like him,” she said. Her first goal, she added, “is to earn back the trust of the people of Minnesota in state government.”

For now, Minnesota Democrats have expressed almost uniform relief that Ms. Klobuchar is their nominee rather than the current governor, Tim Walz.

They began 2026 in panic mode as a scandal over widespread fraud in state-run safety net programs dogged Mr. Walz’s bid for a third term. State lawmakers openly fretted that his name at the top of the ballot in this year’s midterm elections would give Republicans a strong shot at winning the governor’s mansion for the first time in two decades and controlling the tightly divided Legislature.

“I would definitely be lying if I said that the worry meter wasn’t ticking up, up, up by the week,” said State Representative Mike Howard, a Democrat from the Twin Cities.

They exhaled when Mr. Walz dropped his re-election bid in early January, as the Trump administration was sending thousands of immigration agents to the state in what the president called a campaign of “RECKONING & RETRIBUTION.”

Ms. Klobuchar announced her run for governor later that month as Minnesotans were reeling from the killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti, two American citizens shot by immigration agents in Minneapolis. “These times call for grit and resilience,” Ms. Klobuchar proclaimed.

The announcement amounted to a reversal of fortunes for Democrats, making Ms. Klobuchar the clear favorite in the general election race against Lisa Demuth, the Republican speaker of the Minnesota House. Even far-left lawmakers in the State Capitol — where the party has a one-seat majority in the Senate and is tied in the House — have emerged as enthusiastic surrogates for Ms. Klobuchar.

“People in the Democratic Party here in Minnesota understand she’s our best path to winning a majority and defending ourselves from Donald Trump,” said State Senator Zaynab Mohamed, a member of the democratic socialist wing of the party.

Ms. Klobuchar kicked off her run by calling all 101 Democrats in the Legislature, keeping several on the phone for more than an hour. There was talk of campaign strategy, lawmakers said, but Ms. Klobuchar was most interested in their policy goals.

When she ran for president in 2020, Ms. Klobuchar was the subject of several critical articles depicting her as a perfectionist and difficult boss whose office had among the highest turnover in the Senate.

Ms. Klobuchar has a tendency to personally tackle tasks most elected officials delegate and to fire off all-caps emails to aides, which often land in inboxes between midnight and dawn.

Some supporters now call that feverish approach an asset.

Representative Zack Stephenson, the Democratic leader in the Minnesota House, recalled being startled by a 3 a.m. email from Ms. Klobuchar in 2006 when he served as a lowly aide in her first Senate campaign.

“The lesson I took away from that race is that to be successful in politics, the secret is to work really hard,” he said.

The sense of relief extends to Democratic voters like Ms. Carlson, the cheesemaker, who says she has soured on Governor Walz, a former schoolteacher and coach who oversaw the adoption of a raft of progressive policies and made a splash on the national stage by running for vice president in 2024.

In recent years, Ms. Carlson said, small business owners like herself have grown frustrated by tax increases and red tape that seem to grow each year. Then came revelations about rampant fraud in state programs meant to feed low-income children, treat minors with autism and help people at risk of homelessness.

“I just think things got away from him when he did the whole run,” said Ms. Carlson, 54, who lives in Center City, a conservative town 40 miles north of the Twin Cities. “He couldn’t keep a watchful eye, and whoever was wasn’t doing their job.”

She said she hoped Ms. Klobuchar would be different.

That is the senator’s pitch. Having enthusiastically backed Mr. Walz’s vice-presidential bid two years ago, Ms. Klobuchar has now distanced herself from him.

She kicked off her campaign in May by announcing a detailed plan to combat fraud. Evoking the years she served as the elected county prosecutor in Minneapolis, she stood alongside the former U.S. attorney in Minnesota against a backdrop of law books.

“You are right to be angry about the fraud,” Ms. Klobuchar said at the time.

Ms. Klobuchar has also questioned how Governor Walz and allied lawmakers spent a $17 billion surplus in 2023. After Mr. Walz granted a pardon in June to a man convicted of child sexual abuse who was facing deportation to Laos, Ms. Klobuchar said she would have let the conviction stand.

A spokesman for Mr. Walz did not respond to a request for comment.

Ms. Demuth, the Republican candidate for governor, has sought to portray Ms. Klobuchar’s bid as a de facto third term for Mr. Walz, questioning why she wasn’t outspoken about the fraud problem before jumping into the race.

“She will not be able to enact the changes that are desperately needed,” Ms. Demuth said in an interview.

Ms. Klobuchar has called Ms. Demuth a “rubber stamp for Donald Trump.”

But how Ms. Klobuchar will approach the Trump administration — and whether that will satisfy Democrats in a state with a strong leftist streak — remains unclear.

Activists have pressed her to adopt a statewide sanctuary policy for undocumented immigrants, which would ban local jurisdictions from signing cooperation agreements with Immigration and Customs Enforcement. One activist recently confronted Ms. Klobuchar about the issue as she marched in a small town parade.

So far she has refused. In the interview, Ms. Klobuchar, who has long championed a broad overhaul of the immigration system, said she intended to make a case that immigrants are vital to Minnesota’s economic growth.

“I cannot tell you the number of small businesses that we have run by immigrants in our state,” she said.

Ms. Klobuchar trounced a handful of little-known candidates in the Aug. 11 primary, winning nearly 90 percent of the vote. That dominance meant she avoided being meaningfully drawn into fraught policy debates playing out in other national races, said Kobey Layne, 26, a democratic socialist who placed a distant second.

Ms. Layne said she worried that as governor, Ms. Klobuchar would prioritize bipartisan cooperation and incremental change over bold overhauls, such as the creation of a state-run, single-payer health care system.

Asked about the growing clout of democratic socialists, Ms. Klobuchar said she welcomed intraparty policy debates and expected pushback from all sides if elected. She also acknowledged rumors that she was considering appointing Republicans to her cabinet.

“Spoiler alert,” she said. “You’re not going to like everything I do.”

item.title: 5 Races to Watch This Fall for Answers to the Biggest Midterm Questions
item.description:
It’s Labor Day, which for campaigns across the country means the sprint to the November midterm elections is on.

As both parties battle for control of Congress, as well as governorships, here are five races to watch for answers to some of the biggest questions at the center of the midterms, including how attitudes about President Trump and the economy will shape the results, how an insurgent progressive pitch will be received in a battleground contest and more.

IOWA SENATE Race

Iowa has been a reliably red state that Mr. Trump won three times in a row. But this year, Democrats see a chance to turn things around by tapping into economic struggles driven by some of his policies.

The Senate race between Representative Ashley Hinson, a Republican, and State Representative Josh Turek, a Democrat, is testing whether voters in a largely rural, conservative state will turn against Republican candidates over Mr. Trump’s tariffs, which have hit agricultural and manufacturing industries hard, and high fertilizer and gas prices, which have climbed steeply amid the war in Iran.

Ms. Hinson has praised tax cuts passed under Mr. Trump and said his tariffs were necessary to bring trade partners to the table, while pushing back at times on Mr. Trump’s trade policies. Mr. Turek has denounced high costs and blamed Republicans for farmers’ economic challenges.

The race could also determine control of the Senate, which nonpartisan analysts see as increasingly up for grabs.

A Democratic win would represent a breakthrough with voters that the party has struggled to connect with over the past few elections, while a Republican victory would suggest that even amid frustration with the economy, some voters are not ready to break with Mr. Trump and his party.

Texas’ 28th congressional district

A nationwide gerrymandering battle that Mr. Trump and his party started has largely played out in their favor. In Texas, Republicans redrew the Congressional map to gain as many as five House seats. In doing so, they made a bet that Republicans could keep some of the inroads that Mr. Trump made with Latino voters, including in South Texas, in 2024.

One test of the Republican strategy is in the state’s 28th Congressional District, where Representative Henry Cuellar, a moderate Democrat whom Mr. Trump pardoned as he awaited a bribery trial, is seeking re-election against Tano Tijerina, a county judge. The district favored Mr. Trump by about 10 percentage points under its new boundaries and increased the share of Hispanic voters from about 75 percent to about 91 percent.

Since 2024, there have been some indications that Mr. Trump’s support in South Texas is waning amid voter concerns about the economy and immigration crackdowns. And elections held in other states have shown encouraging signs for Democrats in their efforts to improve their standing with Latino voters.

The outcome in the district, along with others in Texas, including the 15th and 34th Congressional Districts, will help determine how effective the Republican Party’s unusual middecade redistricting strategy ends up being and offer fresh indicators of each party’s standing with Latino voters.

Georgia Governor’s race

Democrats are hoping to make gains in the South and win statewide contests in North Carolina and Georgia, where their Senate candidates are currently in strong positions. The open governor’s race in Georgia, one of the most competitive on the map, is another big contest on the minds of leaders in both parties.

Georgia has flipped back and forth during the last three presidential elections, most recently voting for Mr. Trump in 2024, and has hosted competitive Senate races in recent years. But it has not had a Democratic governor since Roy Barnes left office in 2003.

Keisha Lance Bottoms, the Democratic nominee, served in President Joseph R. Biden Jr.’s administration and was his first endorsement of the cycle. If she wins, she would be the first Black woman in U.S. history to be elected governor.

Her Republican opponent is the billionaire health care executive Rick Jackson, who has attacked her record as Atlanta mayor, trying to make her a symbol of unpopular Democratic policies on criminal justice. Ms. Bottoms has sought to tie Mr. Jackson to Mr. Trump. The president’s unpopularity has given Democrats an opening in Southern swing states, but the party has its own brand problems. How Ms. Bottoms does in November will provide a snapshot of its overall standing.

MICHIGAN’s Seventh Congressional District

Progressive insurgents notched some major victories this primary season, largely in safely Democratic territory. In battleground areas, some moderate Democrats (as well as Republicans) have argued that these candidates put their party in a weaker position in the general election, an assertion that will be tested in Michigan’s Seventh Congressional District.

There, Representative Tom Barrett, a vulnerable Republican who has promoted his efforts to limit Mr. Trump’s war powers in Iran, faces a challenge from William Lawrence, a Democrat who co-founded the Sunrise Movement, a youth-led environmental group.

Mr. Barrett has attacked Mr. Lawrence for his past affiliation with the Democratic Socialists of America (Mr. Lawrence said he recently allowed his membership to lapse). Mr. Lawrence has also distanced himself from comments and social media posts he previously made, including some recently unearthed by CNN in which he attacked Democrats and embraced left-wing positions.

Mr. Lawrence has campaigned on opposing data centers and enacting universal health care. Progressives have argued that such issues can energize working-class voters not just in Democratic primaries but in general elections, as well. Republicans across the country, meanwhile, are eager to portray Democrats as too far to the left. The Michigan race is expected to factor into the battle for control of the House this fall. The nonpartisan Cook Political Report rates it as a tossup.

VIRGINIA’S Second congressional district

Mr. Trump’s unpopular war with Iran is a point of contention in plenty of races across the country. It is a particular focal point in the race for Virginia’s Second Congressional District, where two Navy veterans are battling for a seat that has a high concentration of military personnel and the world’s largest Navy base.

Former Representative Elaine Luria, the Democrat, has made opposition to the war a key theme in her bid to retake the seat from Representative Jen Kiggans, the Republican incumbent. Ms. Kiggans has voted repeatedly against resolutions that would limit Mr. Trump’s war powers and has waved off reports of harsh conditions on the Abraham Lincoln, a Navy aircraft carrier, as “democrat lies and misinformation.”

The Cook Political Report sees the race as a tossup. Its outcome will offer a glimpse of how military families, veterans and personnel feel about the war.

item.title: Officials Search for Answers After Fatal Runway Crash in Miami
item.description:
Federal investigators scoured for clues Monday about why a cargo plane failed to stop on a runway at Miami International Airport the day before, resulting in a fiery crash that killed five people. The crash also injured five people, including three critically, and upended holiday travel for hundreds.

The National Transportation Safety Board said it planned to hold a news conference on Monday at 4 p.m. to provide an update. The conditions of the three people who were seriously injured were unclear as of midday Monday.

Officials have not identified the victims, nor specified if those killed were aboard the plane or were on the ground. Some people had been trapped inside their vehicles after the accident, the authorities said.

Videos and images of the crash, as well as information shared by the authorities, establish a broad outline of what occurred on Sunday.

A cargo plane operated for Amazon departed from Luis Muñoz Marín International Airport in San Juan, Puerto Rico, and touched down in Miami just before 2 p.m. But for reasons that remain unclear, the plane overran the runway and plowed into a public road, crashing into multiple vehicles, the authorities said.

Air traffic control audio and emergency dispatch recordings captured the moment of the accident.

“Looks like we have an aircraft that overran the runway,” an air traffic controller said around 2 p.m.

Then, a Miami-Dade Fire Rescue official can be heard saying: “Guys, the plane’s on fire, plane’s on fire. Put your game faces on.”

Videos and photos show the plane skidding across Northwest 67th Avenue, a small public road. The aircraft then plowed into a lot, where it caught fire before coming to a stop beside rows of parked vehicles, covered in smoke. Next to the plane, which had “Prime Air” printed on its side in large blue font, were mangled vehicles.

The crash jolted Miami and its airport, the nation’s busiest for international freight, as many remained ensnared in a maelstrom of travel delays on Monday. At least 153 flights were delayed and 65 canceled by noon on Monday, according to FlightAware, a flight tracking website.

At the airport, many tried to sort out delays from the previous night — and waited.

Finan Herbert Sabaroche, 83, a retired educator, said he was returning from the Caribbean island nation of Dominica, where he was born. He had no guarantees about when he would return home to his wife in Norfolk, Va., as he remained on a standby list from Sunday afternoon.

“I don’t have any problem sleeping here,” Mr. Sabaroche said, noting that he needed to get home soon. He and his wife are scheduled to travel in a few days to attend their grandson’s wedding.

Another traveler, Yony Miranda, 58, of New York City, sat slumped in a chair across from the American Airlines ticket counter. He had spent three weeks on vacation in Colombia and arrived on a stopover in Miami late Sunday. Agents rebooked his flight — but not until Tuesday morning.

“I’m not happy about it,” Mr. Miranda said.

The cargo plane crash also comes at a difficult time for the aviation industry, as a recent series of high-profile accidents in the United States has left many travelers unsettled.

In January 2025, a passenger jet and a U.S. Army helicopter crashed near the Potomac River in Washington, D.C., killing 67 people in the deadliest air crash in the country in 20 years. Last November, a U.P.S. cargo plane crashed in Louisville, Ky., killing 15 people. And in March, a plane collided with a fire truck at LaGuardia Airport in New York City, killing both pilots.

The cause of Sunday’s crash was not immediately apparent. But runway excursions — in which an aircraft overruns or otherwise leaves a runway during takeoff or landing — are the most common type of aviation accident reported annually, according to the International Air Transport Association, a global aviation trade group. They can happen for many reasons, including unstable approaches, runway conditions and crosswinds.

Clouds and thunderstorms were moving through the area around Miami International Airport shortly before the plane landing, according to the National Weather Service. Wind gusts of around 30 miles per hour, which peaked in the minute before the crash, could have affected the landing, aviation experts said.

Amazon Air contracts out its cargo flights. The plane that crashed on Sunday was operated by 21 Air, which operates eight planes for the company.

Keith Winters, the chief executive of 21 Air, which is headquartered in Greensboro, N.C., said in a statement that “we are devastated by the accident involving one of our aircraft,” and that the company was cooperating fully with investigators.

Ali Watkins contributed reporting.
